lesson_title: Why Seven Is the Lucky Number
hook_text: Roll two dice. There are eleven possible totals, 2 to 12. So each total has a 1 in 11 chance? Draw the grid and watch that idea fall apart.
clip_script: Two dice, eleven possible totals from 2 to 12. One in eleven each? No. Draw a grid: first die down the side, 1 to 6, second die across the top, 1 to 6. Thirty-six squares, every one equally likely. Now write the total in each square. How many squares make 2? One: a 1 and a 1. How many make 7? Six: 1 and 6, 2 and 5, 3 and 4, 4 and 3, 5 and 2, 6 and 1, a whole diagonal. So the chance of a 7 is 6 out of 36, which is 1 in 6, and the chance of a 2 is 1 in 36. Seven is six times as likely as two. That is why 7 is the number dice games are built around. The grid shows it in one look, and it works for any two things: a coin and a die, two spinners. When things happen one after another instead, you draw branches and multiply along them. Say it: thirty-six squares, six sevens.
visual_style: A six-by-six grid draws itself on a whiteboard; totals fill the squares; the single 2 glows alone while the six 7s light up along a diagonal; a small bar at the side compares 1 of 36 with 6 of 36.
pacing: The wrong idea fast, the grid building at speaking pace, the counting of sevens one by one, the conclusion with a beat.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson for coin-and-die outcomes, tree diagrams and drawing marbles without replacement.
